title: Human Eye Anatomy: Cornea, Lens, Retina & Visual Nerves
description: Explore human eye anatomy, including the cornea, iris, crystalline lens, ciliary body, vitreous chamber, neural retina, macula, and optic nerve visual map.
h1: Human Eye Anatomy: Cornea, Lens, Chambers, Retina and Optic Nerve
blurb: A self-focusing optical globe: transparent cornea and crystalline lens bend light onto a ten-layered neural retina packed with rod and cone photoreceptors.
lead: Built like a self-focusing biological camera just 24 millimeters wide, the human eye bends incoming light across transparent media onto a neural carpet of photoreceptors. In this illustrated guide to human eye anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including cornea, sclera, choroid, retina—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Built like a self-focusing biological camera just 24 millimeters wide, the human eye bends incoming light across transparent media onto a neural carpet of photoreceptors. Light is refracted mostly at the cornea and finely focused by the lens, whose curvature is changed by the ciliary muscle for near vision. The iris adjusts pupil size to control light entry. The image lands on the retina, where rods (dim light, motion) and cones (colour, detail) convert photons into signals through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons leave as the optic nerve. The fovea, a pit in the macula with cones only, gives sharp central vision. The retina is neural tissue: it is the only place in the body where the central nervous system can be seen directly. Within the human body, the eye (Oculus) is situated in orbit, protected by the bony orbital walls, receives arterial perfusion via ophthalmic artery (central retinal + ciliary branches), and is innervated by optic (II) · motor III, IV, VI · autonomic for pupil.

Structurally, the cornea comprises transparent, avascular, five-layered dome at the front of the eye. Provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power. Physiologically, the cornea bends and transmits light; its endothelium pumps water out to stay clear. The sclera is the tough white outer coat of collagen, continuous with the cornea anteriorly and the dural sheath of the optic nerve posteriorly. Physiologically, the sclera maintains the shape of the globe and anchors the extraocular muscles. The choroid (Choroidea) is the vascular middle layer between sclera and retina, densely packed with capillaries and melanin. Physiologically, the choroid feeds the outer retina and absorbs stray light to sharpen the image. The retina is ten-layered neural film: photoreceptors outermost (light must pass through the inner layers first), then bipolar and ganglion cells. Physiologically, the retina transduces light into nerve impulses. The macula & fovea (Macula lutea) is a 5.5 mm yellow-pigmented area at the posterior pole; its centre, the fovea, contains cones only and no vessels. Physiologically, the macula & fovea governs high-acuity central vision for reading and faces. Structurally, the optic disc (Discus opticus) comprises where ganglion axons and the central retinal vessels pierce the sclera. It has no photoreceptors. Physiologically, the optic disc governs exit point of the optic nerve and entry of the central retinal artery.

Clinically, regarding the cornea, endothelial failure causes oedema and cloudy vision; reshaping the cornea (LASIK) corrects refractive error. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the sclera, thins with age and in inflammation (scleritis, a painful red eye linked to autoimmune disease). In clinical pathology involving the choroid, its high blood flow makes it a common site for metastatic deposits and for uveitis. Medical evaluation of the retina also notes that retinal detachment is a surgical emergency — flashes, floaters and a curtain across the field.

questions.question: How does the eye focus light on the retina?
questions.answer: The cornea provides much of the eye's focusing power, while the lens changes shape for near and far vision. Light is converted into neural signals by retinal photoreceptors.

questions.question: What is the difference between the retina and the optic nerve?
questions.answer: The retina is the light-sensitive neural tissue lining the back of the eye; axons from its ganglion cells converge to form the optic nerve.

questions.question: What is the cornea?
questions.answer: The cornea is a transparent, avascular, five-layered dome at the front of the eye that provides most of the eye’s refractive power.

questions.question: Where is the retina located?
questions.answer: The retina lines the inner back wall of the eye, between the vitreous body and the retinal pigment epithelium, choroid and sclera.

questions.question: Where are the macula and fovea located?
questions.answer: The macula is the central region of the retina; the fovea lies at its center, temporal to the optic disc.
